topics.hook: A warm patch of water off Peru can decide what an Indian farmer earns, and the link took a century to establish.

topics.title: Ramsar sites, biosphere reserves and the overlapping labels
topics.hook: The same patch of marsh can be a national park, a Ramsar site, a biosphere reserve and a World Heritage property at once, under four separate authorities.

topics.title: The islands, the straits and why they are strategic
topics.hook: India's southernmost point is not in Tamil Nadu, and its only active volcano is nowhere near the mainland.

topics.title: Gandhi’s three mass movements and what triggered each
topics.hook: Non-Cooperation in 1920, Civil Disobedience in 1930, Quit India in 1942. Three movements, three triggers, three different ways of ending.

topics.title: The Revolt of 1857 and the end of Company rule
topics.hook: Started by sepoys over a rifle cartridge, spread into a rebellion of dispossessed rulers, and ended with the Crown taking India over directly.

topics.title: The Congress: founding, the sessions that matter, and the 1907 split
topics.hook: Founded by a retired British civil servant in 1885, split at Surat in 1907, reunited at Lucknow in 1916, and led by a different person almost every year.

topics.title: From Cripps to Partition: the missions, plans and the Act of 1947
topics.hook: Four attempts to settle the constitutional question in five years, and the one that finally worked did it by dividing the country.

topics.title: Company rule: Plassey, Buxar, and how land revenue was settled
topics.hook: A battle won by bribery in 1757, a battle won properly in 1764, and three revenue systems that shaped rural India for two centuries.

topics.title: Social and religious reform movements and their founders
topics.hook: A matching question waiting to happen: nine movements, nine founders, nine years, and the reforms each of them pushed through.

topics.title: Ancient India: Harappa to the Guptas
topics.hook: A civilisation with drains and no temples, an emperor who gave up war after winning one, and a dynasty whose gold coins are the standard exam question.

topics.title: India after 1947: reorganisation, wars and the Emergency
topics.hook: Linguistic states drawn after a hunger strike, four wars, one Emergency, and the sequence of Prime Ministers the paper expects in order.

topics.title: Medieval India: five Sultanate dynasties and six Mughals
topics.hook: A slave who became a king, a sultan who moved his capital twice and moved it back, and an emperor who could not read.

topics.title: Art and culture: the eight dances, the schools of architecture and the lists
topics.hook: The Sangeet Natak Akademi recognises eight classical dances, and the argument about the ninth has been running for years.

topics.title: Three revolutions and the vocabulary they left behind
topics.hook: Liberty, equality and fraternity reached the Preamble of the Indian Constitution by way of a Paris street in 1789.

topics.title: The two world wars and the institutions built out of them
topics.hook: The treaty that ended the first war is widely blamed for causing the second, and the man who said so at the time was an economist nobody listened to.

topics.title: The Cold War, non-alignment and the end of empire
topics.hook: India refused to pick a side and then organised everyone else who refused too.

topics.title: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and the amendment cases before it
topics.hook: Thirteen judges, sixty-eight days of hearing, eleven separate opinions and a 7-6 split that decided Parliament can amend the Constitution but cannot rewrite what it is.

topics.title: SR Bommai v Union of India and Article 356
topics.hook: The Supreme Court restricted the arbitrary use of Article 356 by the central government, establishing federalism and secularism as basic features.

topics.title: Maneka Gandhi (1978) and the golden triangle
topics.hook: A passport impounded "in the public interest" without reasons, and the judgment that turned Article 21 from a formality into the most powerful provision in the Constitution.

topics.title: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v Shah Bano Begum and Muslim Personal Law
topics.hook: The Supreme Court upheld a divorced Muslim woman's right to maintenance under Section 125 of the CrPC, sparking a political backlash and legislative override.

topics.title: Shayara Bano v Union of India and the End of Triple Talaq
topics.hook: A five-judge bench struck down the practice of instant triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat) as unconstitutional and arbitrary.

topics.title: Vishaka v State of Rajasthan and Workplace Harassment Guidelines
topics.hook: In the absence of legislation, the Supreme Court laid down binding guidelines to prevent and redress sexual harassment of women at the workplace.

topics.title: KS Puttaswamy v Union of India and the Right to Privacy
topics.hook: A unanimous nine-judge bench ruled that the right to privacy is an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21.

topics.title: The statutes a legal GK paper assumes you know
topics.hook: Most legal GK questions are not about cases. They are about which Act covers what, and how many days you have.

topics.title: Indra Sawhney (1992): reservation, the creamy layer and the 50% ceiling
topics.hook: The Mandal case. Nine judges, 27% for other backward classes upheld, promotions excluded, and a ceiling that Parliament has since gone around twice.

topics.title: Navtej Singh Johar (2018) and the dismantling of Victorian morality
topics.hook: Section 377 was drafted by Macaulay in 1860 and read down in 2018 by five judges who described the earlier decision restoring it as a mistake the Court had to correct.

topics.title: Contract, tort and crime: the principles legal reasoning runs on
topics.hook: A legal reasoning question gives you the rule. What it tests is whether you will apply the rule you were given rather than the one you half remember.

topics.title: The three new criminal laws that replaced the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act
topics.hook: From 1 July 2024 India stopped prosecuting under an 1860 code. The names, the dates and what replaced what are guaranteed exam material.

topics.title: Doctrines and maxims a law entrance expects you to know
topics.hook: Fifteen terms that turn up in legal reasoning passages, in questions on judgments, and in the reading comprehension section without warning.

topics.title: The United Nations: Charter, six organs, and 193 members
topics.hook: The UN Charter was signed in San Francisco in 1945 by 51 states and set up six organs; eighty years later membership has nearly quadrupled to 193, one of those six organs has gone dormant, and the whole structure is the base layer for almost every other body this section covers.

topics.title: The Security Council: the veto, the P5, and India's push for a seat
topics.hook: Fifteen countries sit on the Security Council, but only five can single-handedly stop it from acting, and that veto power has shaped nearly every major international crisis since 1945, including India's decades-long campaign for a permanent seat of its own.

topics.title: UN specialised agencies: founding year, headquarters, and what each one does
topics.hook: The single most mechanically examined table in general knowledge. Learn the city and the year and you can answer most of what is asked.

topics.title: Regional groupings: who is in, who founded them, and where the last summit was
topics.hook: BRICS, G20, QUAD, SCO, ASEAN, SAARC, BIMSTEC. Membership lists that change, and the changes are exactly what gets asked.

topics.title: Bretton Woods: the Fund, the Bank and the trade body that took fifty years
topics.hook: Two institutions were agreed in three weeks at a New Hampshire hotel in 1944. The third took until 1995.

topics.title: Environmental treaties: the conventions, their years and their host cities
topics.hook: Stockholm to Kunming-Montreal, with a protocol named after every city that hosted a conference. The years and the gases are what get asked.

topics.title: The international courts and what each one can actually do
topics.hook: One court tries states, another tries people, and they sit in the same city without any connection between them.

topics.title: The Preamble and the basic structure doctrine
topics.hook: The Preamble is the Constitution stating its own purpose, and the basic structure doctrine is the Supreme Court deciding that purpose cannot be amended away.

topics.title: Fundamental Rights: Part III, Articles 12 to 35
topics.hook: Six rights, one definition clause, one clause that voids inconsistent laws, and a remedy the Constitution itself calls its heart.

topics.title: Article 21: how one sentence became the whole of Indian rights law
topics.hook: "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." Twenty-two words that now carry privacy, a clean environment, education, livelihood and the right to die with dignity.

topics.title: Article 32, Article 226 and the five writs
topics.hook: Five Latin names, two articles, and one distinction the exam asks about every year: the Supreme Court writ is a Fundamental Right, the High Court writ is wider.

topics.title: Article 14 and the two tests of equality
topics.hook: Equality before the law is British, equal protection of the laws is American, and Indian courts read the same article two different ways depending on which test they reach for.

topics.title: Emergency provisions: Articles 352, 356 and 360
topics.hook: Three kinds of emergency, one of which has been used more than a hundred times and one of which has never been used at all.

topics.title: Parliament: two Houses, and the money bill that only one of them controls
topics.hook: The Lok Sabha can be dissolved and the Rajya Sabha cannot, the Rajya Sabha can only delay a money bill by fourteen days, and the Speaker decides what a money bill is.

topics.title: The judiciary: appointments, the collegium and the NJAC that never was
topics.hook: Judges appointing judges is not in the Constitution. It is the result of three cases, and Parliament’s attempt to undo it lasted eleven months.

topics.title: Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties
topics.hook: Non-justiciable instructions to the State, borrowed from Ireland, that courts have used anyway to decide what Article 21 means.

topics.title: Constitutional, statutory and executive bodies: the distinction they always test
topics.hook: The Election Commission is constitutional, the NHRC is statutory, and NITI Aayog is neither. Getting that sorting right is worth more marks than knowing what any of them do.

topics.title: Federalism and the Seventh Schedule
topics.hook: Three lists, one residuary power, and a Constitution that calls itself a Union of States rather than a federation.

topics.title: The President: election, powers and the ordinance route
topics.hook: Elected by an electoral college that includes no ordinary voter, bound by ministerial advice since 1976, and able to legislate for six weeks at a time when Parliament is not sitting.

topics.title: Amending the Constitution, and the amendments worth knowing by number
topics.hook: Three procedures, one of which is not even in Article 368, and about a dozen amendment numbers that carry most of the marks.

topics.title: Making the Constitution, and what was borrowed from where
topics.hook: Two years, eleven months and eighteen days, 389 members at the start, and a document that openly took its best ideas from eight other countries.

topics.title: Anti-defection and the Tenth Schedule
topics.hook: A law meant to stop horse-trading that now turns on how fast a Speaker chooses to decide.

topics.title: Local government: the 73rd and 74th Amendments
topics.hook: Constitutional status for the third tier, a fixed five-year term, and a third of all seats reserved for women.

topics.title: Citizenship: Articles 5 to 11 and the Citizenship Act
topics.hook: The Constitution deals only with who was a citizen in 1950. Everything since is ordinary law, which is why citizenship can be changed without amending the Constitution.

topics.title: Article 19: the six freedoms and the eight grounds for restricting them
topics.hook: Six freedoms for citizens only, each with its own list of reasonable restrictions, and one clause added in 1951 because the courts had struck down press censorship.

topics.title: Elections: the Commission, the law and the reforms that came from court
topics.hook: A constitutional body with three members, a code of conduct with no statutory force that everyone obeys anyway, and a string of reforms the Supreme Court ordered rather than Parliament passing.

topics.title: ISRO: the missions, the launch vehicles and the people
topics.hook: Chandrayaan-3 made India the first country to land near the lunar south pole, and the fourth to soft-land at all. The rest of the programme is a list worth memorising.

topics.title: The nuclear and missile programme, and the treaties India refuses to sign
topics.hook: Two test sites, one three-stage plan built around thorium, and a consistent refusal to join the two treaties everyone asks about.

topics.title: Health and disease: the vocabulary a passage assumes you have
topics.hook: Which disease is caused by which agent, which vitamin deficiency causes what, and the difference between an epidemic and a pandemic.

topics.title: Climate science and the treaties built on it
topics.hook: One treaty on an atmospheric problem worked completely, and it is not the one anybody talks about.

topics.title: Everyday science: units, phenomena and who discovered what
topics.hook: Why the sky is blue, why a stick looks bent in water, and the list of scientist-to-discovery pairs that gets asked without warning.

topics.title: The digital state: Aadhaar, UPI, data law and the AI question
topics.hook: A biometric number, a payments rail and a data statute, each of which was litigated before it was finished.
